section.title: Why Do You Stand Far Off
section.sectionRationale: The second half of the acrostic begun in Psalm 9, an urgent lament over the arrogant wicked who prey on the helpless while God seems distant, resolving in confident trust that the LORD is King forever and hears the desire of the humble.
section.thesis: Though the wicked boast, deny God, and prey on the helpless as if He does not see, David appeals to the LORD, who does see trouble and grief, to rise and act as King forever, breaking the arm of the wicked and vindicating the fatherless and oppressed.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the opening cry over God's apparent distance (vv1-2), a detailed portrait of the wicked's arrogance and predation on the helpless (vv3-11), a plea for God to arise and remember (vv12-15), and the closing confession of the LORD's eternal kingship and care for the oppressed (vv16-18).

units.label: Why do You stand far off
units.note: why do You hide in times of trouble

verses.text: Why, O LORD, do You stand far off? Why do You hide in times of trouble?
In pride the wicked pursue the needy; let them be caught in the schemes they devise.
For the wicked man boasts in the cravings of his heart; he blesses the greedy and reviles the LORD.
In his pride the wicked man does not seek Him; in all his schemes there is no God.
He is secure in his ways at all times; Your lofty judgments are far from him; he sneers at all his foes.
He says to himself, "I will not be moved; from age to age I am free of distress."
His mouth is full of cursing, deceit, and violence; trouble and malice are under his tongue.
He lies in wait near the villages; in ambush he slays the innocent; his eyes watch in stealth for the helpless.
He lies in wait like a lion in a thicket; he lurks to seize the oppressed; he catches the lowly in his net.
They are crushed and beaten down; the hapless fall prey to his strength.
He says to himself, "God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees."

units.label: Arise, O Lord
units.note: You have regarded trouble and grief

verses.text: Arise, O LORD! Lift up Your hand, O God! Do not forget the helpless.
Why has the wicked man renounced God? He says to himself, "You will never call me to account."
But You have regarded trouble and grief; You see to repay it by Your hand. The victim entrusts himself to You; You are the helper of the fatherless.
Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call him to account for his wickedness until none is left to be found.

units.label: The Lord is King forever
units.note: to vindicate the fatherless and oppressed

verses.text: The LORD is King forever and ever; the nations perish from His land.
You have heard, O LORD, the desire of the {{anavim|humble}}; You will strengthen their hearts. You will incline Your ear,
to vindicate the fatherless and oppressed, that the men of the earth may strike terror no more.

anavim.gloss: The humble, the afflicted or lowly, those bent low by hardship who look to God rather than their own strength. The LORD's ear is inclined precisely to this desire, forming a pattern across the Psalms where God favors the humble over the proud, later echoed in the Beatitudes, Matthew 5:5.

basic.context: Psalm 10 continues the acrostic begun in Psalm 9, but its tone shifts sharply to lament. David cries out that God seems to stand far off while the arrogant wicked prey on the helpless and deny that God even sees. The psalm resolves in confidence that the LORD is King forever, who hears the desire of the humble and vindicates the fatherless.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm gives voice to the painful gap between God's promised justice and its apparent delay, refusing to pretend the wicked's success is not troubling; it teaches that naming this tension honestly to God, rather than suppressing it, is itself an act of faith, since the psalm ends in confident trust rather than despair.
basic.originalLanguages: The wicked man's inner monologue, God has forgotten, He hides His face and never sees, is quoted twice, a rhetorical device exposing the practical atheism behind arrogant oppression. By contrast, the LORD hears the desire of the anavim, the humble or afflicted, those who have nothing to rely on but Him.
basic.typology: David's plea that God rise, break the arm of the wicked, and vindicate the fatherless anticipates the final judgment Christ will bring, when every arrogant claim that God does not see will be answered in full.
basic.christ: Jesus is God's answer to the cry 'why do You stand far off'; in the incarnation God draws near to exactly the helpless and fatherless this psalm describes, and at His return He will fully break the power of every arrogant evildoer described here.
basic.god: God appears distant to the sufferer's experience, yet the psalm insists He does in fact regard trouble and grief and will repay it by His hand, holding together honest complaint about felt divine absence with unwavering confidence in God's actual attentiveness and coming justice.
basic.crossReferences: James 1:27 defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows in their affliction, echoing this psalm's concern for the fatherless. Matthew 5:5 blesses the meek, echoing God's care for the anavim. Psalm 34:18 promises the LORD is near the brokenhearted.
basic.oneStory: Psalm 10 gives every believer permission to ask honestly why God seems distant while evil flourishes, and answers that question not with an explanation but with a person: the King who reigns forever, who draws near to the helpless in Jesus Christ and will finally silence every arrogant denial that He sees.

context.literary:
Psalm 10 is the second half of the alphabetic pair, and it is the mirror of Psalm 9 in more than its mood. Psalm 9 spoke of the nations and the wicked as a company under judgment; Psalm 10 zooms in on one wicked man and follows him from his heart to his mouth to his hands. The portrait in verses 3 to 11 is the longest sustained character study of an oppressor in the Psalter, and it is built as a descent. Verses 3 to 6 show his inner life, boasting and denying God. Verse 7 opens his mouth. Verses 8 to 10 show his hands at work in ambush. Verse 11 brings us back to his heart, closing the circle with his private creed, 'God has forgotten.'

The structure is a frame around that portrait. The psalm opens with a 'why' addressed to God, verse 1, and it closes with an affirmation addressed to God, verses 16 to 18. In between the poet does something unusual. He turns from speaking to God, verses 1 and 2, to speaking about the wicked man for nine verses, and only turns back to God with the command 'Arise, O LORD,' verse 12. The reader is made to sit with the oppressor's voice long enough to feel the danger before prayer resumes.

The wicked man's quoted words come twice, in verses 6 and 11, and once more in a rhetorical question, verse 13. The poet lets him speak so that his theology can be heard. Against those quotes the psalm sets its own answer in verse 14, which begins with the emphatic 'But You,' and in verses 16 to 18, which end with the LORD as king. The poem moves from a question to a declaration without ever explaining why God delayed. The resolution is not an argument but a change of address, from complaint to confession.
context.historical:
There is no heading on this psalm in the Hebrew, which is unusual in the first book of the Psalter, where nearly every psalm is attributed to David. That absence fits the sense that it continues Psalm 9 and shares its author. The setting is never stated, and that silence lets the psalm speak to any age of unchecked oppression.

The world behind it is rural and unprotected. The wicked man lies in wait 'near the villages,' verse 8, the unwalled hamlets that had no gate or garrison, where a lone family was exposed to bandits and predatory landowners. In such a setting the helpless, those with no brother or clan to defend them, were easy prey. The lion in his thicket, verse 9, is an image the first hearers would have known from the hills of Judah, and the net is the hunter's and the fowler's tool.

The word for 'fatherless' carries legal weight. In Israel the orphan and the widow were protected by a specific law and by God Himself as their defender, Exodus 22:22 to 24 and Deuteronomy 10:18. Without a father there was no one to bring a case at the gate or to buy back a family's land. When the prophets later condemn Israel, this is the charge they repeat again and again, Isaiah 1:17 and Malachi 3:5. The psalm asks the LORD to be the family that the victim lacks.

The line 'the nations perish from His land,' verse 16, places God's kingship in the land He gave Israel. It recalls the promise that the land would be cleansed of those who did not honour Him. And the closing wish, that 'the men of the earth may strike terror no more,' verse 18, suggests a time when foreign or local tyrants terrorised the countryside, when men of violence acted as though the God of Israel did not see. The psalm gives the powerless a prayer to say when no human court will listen.
context.canonical:
Psalm 10 is the first of the Psalter's great laments over God's apparent distance, and its opening question, 'Why, O LORD, do You stand far off?' sets the tone for many that follow. Psalm 13 asks 'How long will You hide Your face from me?' and Psalm 44:24 asks 'Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression?' Psalm 22 raises the same voice to its highest pitch, 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?' and then answers in verse 24, 'He has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help.' Psalm 10 begins that conversation, and its own answer, that He has seen and will repay, is the pattern the others follow.

The wicked man's private creed has parallels across Scripture. 'The LORD does not see' is on the lips of the wicked in Psalm 94:7 and of Israel's own elders in Ezekiel 8:12. 'How can God know?' is in Psalm 73:11, and Job's friend imagines the same in Job 22:13. Scripture treats this as the practical atheism that lies under all oppression, and it takes the wicked man's words seriously enough to quote them so that they can be answered.

Other prophets voice the psalm's complaint, Habakkuk 1:2 to 4 and Jeremiah 12:1, and the New Testament shows it enduring. Paul quotes the psalm's description of the wicked mouth, 'full of cursing and bitterness,' Romans 3:14, drawing on Psalm 10:7 in his catena of texts about universal sin. The martyrs under the altar of Revelation ask the psalm's question, 'How long,' Revelation 6:10. And Jesus answers the psalm's assumption that God is far away by telling His disciples that the Father will bring justice for those who cry to Him day and night, Luke 18:7. The psalm ends with God as king, and Revelation ends with the same acclamation, Revelation 11:15.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted his hearers to have a way to pray when God appears absent. The psalm does not answer the question 'why' with an explanation. It gives an example of how faith speaks. The first thing the poem does is direct the complaint to God, 'Why, O LORD,' before it says a word about the wicked. Grief is turned into prayer before it can turn into bitterness or into revenge.

He also meant to expose the anatomy of oppression. The portrait in verses 3 to 11 is an analysis of how injustice works, in three stages. It starts with a heart that cannot bear to be accountable, 'in all his schemes there is no God,' verse 4. It goes on to a mouth that lies and curses, verse 7. And it ends in hands that catch the poor, verses 8 to 10. He intends the listener to see that behind a violent act lies a theology, and that the theology is 'God does not see.'

The psalm has a pastoral aim for the victim as well. The one who is crushed and beaten down, verse 10, is invited to see that the wicked man's confidence is a mistake. 'But You have regarded trouble and grief,' verse 14. The one who is at risk of despair is told that he is not invisible, and the last verses turn his fear into steadiness: 'You will strengthen their hearts.'

Finally, the psalm calls the community to identify with the fatherless. The refrain of the psalm's petitions is that God 'not forget the helpless,' verse 12, and that He vindicate the fatherless, verse 18. The song is for the whole assembly to sing on behalf of the vulnerable, so that those who are safe learn to pray for those who are not.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The long portrait of the wicked man is description, not instruction. The psalm records what a proud oppressor says and does, so that God's people can recognise it and pray against it. It does not commend his ambush and his net, and it certainly does not encourage the reader to answer in kind. The wish that he be caught in his own schemes, verse 2, is placed in God's hands.

The prayers in the psalm are the part that carries forward. Believers are invited to say honestly to God 'why do You stand far off,' and the psalm's own shape shows that this is legitimate speech. They are also invited to plead for the helpless, and the psalm gives the words. But the psalm does not say that God will always appear quickly, and it does not make His nearness depend on our feelings. Its closing confidence is stated, not commanded.

There is also a practical implication that the psalm implies rather than states. The God who is the helper of the fatherless, verse 14, uses His people to do it. Isaiah 1:17 and James 1:27 make explicit what Psalm 10 asks God to do, and so the description of God's care becomes a summons to those who bear His name. A reader who prays verse 18 should be prepared to be part of the answer.

debates.question: Does asking 'why do You stand far off' represent a lapse in David's faith?

views.label: An honest, faith-filled complaint, not a lapse
views.case: The Psalms repeatedly model this kind of direct questioning as legitimate prayer, and this very psalm ends in confident trust, showing the complaint was a step toward, not away from, deeper faith.

views.label: A description of genuine spiritual struggle that the psalm itself resolves
views.case: The sharp tonal shift from Psalm 9's confidence to this psalm's anguish suggests real fluctuation in the psalmist's felt experience of God, which Scripture includes without condemning, ultimately resolved by remembering God's kingship rather than by denying the struggle occurred.

debates.bearing: Either reading affirms that voicing the felt distance of God is legitimate, Spirit-shaped prayer, not evidence of unbelief, especially when, as here, it moves toward renewed trust rather than settling into despair.

debates.question: Who is the wicked man of verses 2 to 11?

views.label: A type, standing for every proud oppressor
views.case: The verbs are singular yet the setting is general, and the psalm shifts freely between 'the wicked man' and 'they' in verse 10. It never names a person or a nation. This makes the portrait a description of a kind of person that any age can recognise, and it explains how the psalm has been prayed by the oppressed of every century.

views.label: A specific enemy of the psalmist
views.case: Some read the details of ambush near villages and of violence against 'the innocent' as pointing to a historical figure, an official or a brigand chief, whom the first singer knew. The Psalter elsewhere names such enemies as Saul or Doeg in its headings, and the lack of a heading here leaves the question open.

views.label: A corporate picture of the nations or of an oppressive class
views.case: Because the psalm's second half speaks of 'the nations' perishing from the LORD's land, verse 16, and because Psalm 9 concerns the nations, some see the wicked man as the collective voice of a hostile power or of the powerful elite within Israel.

debates.bearing: All three readings reach the same practical place. The psalm teaches the reader to recognise the theology beneath oppression, that God does not see, and to pray against it. The identification of the man matters less than the identification of the lie.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm turns on one verb, darash, 'to seek, to inquire, to require,' and it uses it as a hinge between the two psalms. In Psalm 9:10 the LORD has not forsaken 'those who seek You,' and in 9:12 the one who 'avenges' is literally the seeker of blood. In Psalm 10:4 the wicked man 'does not seek Him.' In 10:13 he says 'You will never call me to account,' with the same verb in the negative, and in 10:15 the prayer asks that God 'call him to account,' the same verb again. The wicked man does not seek God and assumes God will not seek him. The psalm answers that the God who is sought by the humble also seeks out the guilty.

Verse 4 begins with a phrase that is literally 'the height of his nose,' gobah appo, and the BSB renders it 'in his pride.' The Hebrew idiom pictures the chin and nose lifted in disdain. Verse 3 has a word that is hard to translate, the verb barak, which usually means 'bless.' Here the sense may be either 'he blesses the greedy' or, as in some translations, that he renounces the LORD, since the verb is sometimes used as a euphemism for cursing God, as in Job 2:9 and 1 Kings 21:13. The BSB has 'blesses the greedy and reviles the LORD,' which keeps both options open.

The wicked man's own inner speech is marked three times with the formula 'he says to himself,' verses 6, 11 and 13, literally 'in his heart.' The same idiom introduces the fool who says 'There is no God,' Psalm 14:1. The Hebrew heart is the place of thought and will, so this is a stated intention, a decision to treat God as not there.

In verses 8 to 10 the vocabulary of predation is dense. The hunter 'lies in wait,' verse 8, and the same verb returns in verse 9, where he 'lies in wait like a lion in a thicket.' The net in verse 9 is resheth, the word used of the snare into which the nations fall in Psalm 9:15. The BSB footnote to verse 10 records that the Hebrew may also be read as 'He crouches and lies low,' one of the psalm's textual difficulties. Either way, the wording evokes an animal hunting.

Verse 14 has 'But You have regarded trouble and grief.' The verb 'see' is emphatic, and the noun pair 'trouble and grief' names the two things the wicked says God cannot see. The victim in the same verse 'entrusts himself to You.' The verb is azav, which means to leave or abandon, the same verb as in Psalm 9:10 where God has not 'forsaken' those who seek Him. A play of leaving runs through the two psalms: God does not leave the seekers, and so the victim can leave himself with God.

Verse 17 says the LORD will 'strengthen' the hearts of the humble. The verb is kun, 'to establish,' the verb of Psalm 9:7 where God has 'established His throne.' God establishes His throne and He establishes His people's hearts. The adjective 'humble,' anavim, is the plural of a word for the poor and lowly who depend on God, and it names those Jesus called meek. Verse 18 ends with the same word for man that ended Psalm 9, enosh, 'the men of the earth,' a frail creature who cannot keep on striking terror.

typology.type: The afflicted one who entrusts himself to God, Psalm 10:14
typology.fulfillment: The victim leaves himself with the LORD and is not disappointed. Jesus is the fullest form of that pattern. 'When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate,' Peter writes, 'He entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. His last words, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' Luke 23:46, are the psalm's verb in action. Where the psalm's victim is at the mercy of a predator, Jesus chose to lay down His life, John 10:18. The correspondence fails at one place: the psalm's victim hopes to be rescued from death, and Jesus goes into death and is raised.

typology.type: The helper of the fatherless, Psalm 10:14 and 18
typology.fulfillment: The LORD steps in as the family the orphan lacks. Jesus says to His disciples, 'I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you,' John 14:18, and Paul says believers received the Spirit of sonship, by whom they cry 'Abba, Father,' Romans 8:15. The escalation is that God does not merely defend the fatherless from a distance but makes them His children. James takes the same step in practice, calling the care of orphans the mark of pure religion, James 1:27. The type falls short in that the psalm imagines vindication in a case at law, while Christ gives adoption into the household.

typology.type: The King forever who vindicates the oppressed, Psalm 10:16 to 18
typology.fulfillment: The psalm ends on the LORD as king forever and the end of terror on the earth. The New Testament sets that kingship in Christ. When the seventh trumpet sounds the kingdom of the world becomes 'the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever,' Revelation 11:15. Paul says Christ 'must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet,' 1 Corinthians 15:25. Isaiah's servant is sent 'to preach good news to the poor,' Isaiah 61:1, and Jesus reads that scroll of Himself, Luke 4:18 to 21. The type is still incomplete, since the terror of the wicked has not yet ceased.

study.christ:
The psalm begins with a question that Jesus Himself asks. 'Why, O LORD, do You stand far off?' is the voice of Psalm 22:1, 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?' which Jesus cries from the cross, Matthew 27:46. The Son has taken the question of every crushed person into His own mouth. The complaint of Psalm 10 is not an outsider's protest; it is a prayer that Christ prayed at the point of deepest pain. And the same Psalm 22 answers, 'He has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help,' verse 24, so the answer of resurrection stands behind the complaint.

The psalm leads to Christ by the figure of the helpless and the fatherless. God's chosen way to be near to the vulnerable was to become vulnerable. The Word 'became flesh,' John 1:14. The one who was born in a stable and lived under an occupying empire, who was falsely accused and beaten, is not a distant God looking on from the sky. In Hebrews He is the high priest who 'sympathizes with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15. Jesus also identifies Himself with the least, 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me,' Matthew 25:40, so that in the ambush of the poor the one waylaid is Christ.

The psalm also anticipates Christ as the one who arises. 'Arise, O LORD! Lift up Your hand,' verse 12, is the prayer for God to act, and the New Testament says He did. In the resurrection God raised Jesus, Acts 2:24, and the Lord Jesus 'will be revealed from heaven,' to 'repay with affliction those who afflict you,' 2 Thessalonians 1:6 and 7. The plea to 'break the arm of the wicked' is answered at the last, and until then the promise of Luke 18:7 stands, that God will bring justice for those who cry to Him day and night.

There is a contrast that is worth naming. The wicked man is a lion in a thicket who preys on the lowly, verse 9. The Bible knows a lion of another kind, 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah,' who 'has triumphed,' Revelation 5:5, and who is at once the Lamb who was slain, verse 6. The predator takes the weak; the true Lion lays down His life for the weak. Peter warns that the adversary 'prowls around like a roaring lion,' 1 Peter 5:8, which shows how deeply the psalm's imagery has been absorbed.

As with all the Psalms, the reading of Christ here must be honest. Psalm 10 is not a coded prophecy of Jesus, and its wicked man is not to be turned into any single figure. But its longing, that the fatherless be vindicated and terror end, is the longing that Christ answers, and the New Testament shows it doing so.
study.god:
Psalm 10 teaches what God is like by starting with what it feels like when He seems absent. The doctrine of God that emerges is not a set of tidy statements but a tested conviction. He is near even when He seems far, and the psalm is willing to say that both experiences are real for the believer. The distance is felt and not actual. 'You stand far off' is the sufferer's perception, and 'You have regarded trouble and grief' is the psalm's verdict.

God sees. That is the crux of the psalm. The wicked man's whole system depends on believing God does not see and will not call him to account. The psalm answers with the verb of vision, 'You see to repay it by Your hand,' verse 14, and with the promise of hearing, 'You have heard, O LORD, the desire of the humble,' verse 17. The God of the Bible is not a spectator. His knowledge is bound to His action: to see trouble is to take it in hand. This is why Scripture treats practical atheism as the deepest cause of cruelty, since any people who believe no one is watching will not restrain themselves.

God is king forever. The psalm's last movement affirms 'The LORD is King forever and ever,' verse 16. That kingship sits above the whole span of the poem, from the apparent silence at the start to the vindication at the end, and it is stated as a fact before the wicked are dealt with. The psalm gives no timetable. It gives an identity.

God is the helper of the fatherless. Many ancient gods were gods of the powerful, of kings and armies. The LORD is presented as the special defender of the helpless, 'You are the helper of the fatherless,' verse 14. His power is not merely large; it is aimed at the weak. He is the one who inclines His ear, verse 17, a picture of a great one bending down to a small voice. That image of condescension in the psalm is the seed of the whole biblical picture of a God who stoops.

God strengthens hearts. The psalm does not promise that the humble will escape every blow but that God will establish their hearts, verse 17. A part of His answer to distress is inner: steadiness before the outward vindication arrives.

For worship, the psalm teaches that honest lament is a form of praise, because it takes God seriously enough to bring Him the whole complaint. It teaches too that faith does not wait for feeling. The psalm moves from 'why' to 'King forever' without the circumstances having changed, and worship is what happens in that movement. The God the psalm meets can bear our questions, and that is one of the deepest things it teaches about Him.

crossReferences.note: The nations fall into a pit of their own making and are caught in the net they hid. Psalm 10:9 shows the wicked man setting the same net for the lowly. Read together, they show the world's oppressor building the very trap in which he will be caught, and the two psalms are the two sides of one picture.

The great psalm of the forsaken says He has not hidden His face from the afflicted but has attended to his cry. It is the reply to Psalm 10:1, where God seems to hide. The cry of the sufferer is heard, and the psalm says so in words that answer the very complaint of the earlier prayer.

The wicked say the LORD does not see and the God of Jacob pays no heed. It repeats the boast of Psalm 10:11, and the psalm answers with a question about whether the God who made the eye can fail to see. It confirms that the denial of God's sight is the standard creed of the oppressor.

The LORD executes justice for the fatherless and widow. This is the law behind Psalm 10:14 and 18. The psalm is asking God to be what He has already said He is, and the plea rests on His revealed character, not on the singer's need alone.

The orphan and the widow are not to be mistreated, and if they cry out God will surely hear. This is the covenant promise that Psalm 10:17 relies on when it says the LORD has heard the desire of the humble. It shows that the psalm's confidence is not wishful but promissory.

Paul weaves together lines from the Psalms about lying tongues and mouths full of cursing to show that sin touches every human being. His words 'full of cursing and bitterness' draw on Psalm 10:7, and the BSB footnote to that verse notes the citation. The psalm's portrait of the wicked becomes a mirror for all.

The prophet cries how long he must call for help and asks why God tolerates wrongdoing. It is the same complaint as Psalm 10:1 from a later age, and the book's answer, that the righteous live by faith, teaches the same lesson as the psalm's turn to trust.

God's people are told to seek justice and defend the fatherless. Where Psalm 10 asks God to be the defender, Isaiah calls the people to share in that work. It shows that prayer for the helpless and action on their behalf belong together.

Pure religion is to look after orphans and widows in their distress. It is the practical outworking of the psalm's picture of God, and it shows the early church reading the fatherless of the Psalter as an ongoing charge and not an ancient category.

Jesus teaches that God will bring justice for His chosen who cry to Him day and night, and will not delay. It is the New Testament reply to Psalm 10's 'Why do You hide,' saying that the apparent delay is not indifference and that the answer is promised.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 10 gives voice to one of the oldest questions in the story. If God made a good world and rules it, why does violence flourish? The first murder came in Genesis 4, when Cain attacked Abel in the field, Genesis 4:8, and the ambush and slaying of the innocent in verses 8 to 10 recall that scene. The oppressor of Psalm 10 is a descendant of Cain, and his creed, that God will never call him to account, is the same one Cain tested when he asked, 'Am I my brother's keeper?' Genesis 4:9. God's answer there was to hear the blood of the victim crying from the ground, Genesis 4:10, and the psalm's confidence that God hears the cry of the helpless is rooted in that first scene.

The story then follows a people who were themselves once the fatherless. In Egypt Israel was crushed and beaten down, and God 'heard their groaning,' Exodus 2:24. The Exodus became the pattern of God's answer to the cry of the oppressed, and the law's care for the orphan and the widow is grounded in it, Deuteronomy 10:18 and 19. When Israel forgot that history and became an oppressor, the prophets called her back, Amos 2:6 and 7. Psalm 10 sits on that line: God is the one who sees and remembers the powerless because He has done so before.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, who does not stand far off. He enters the world as the helpless, is crushed under the wicked, and cries the psalm's question from the cross. His resurrection answers it. And He gives to His people what the fatherless lacked: the Spirit of adoption, Romans 8:15, a family and a Father. The church is meant to share in that work, so that the psalm's prayer for the fatherless becomes a mission.

The story ends with the psalm's last verse fulfilled. God will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The seventh trumpet proclaims the kingdom of the world to be our Lord's, Revelation 11:15. The questions of the Psalter, 'why' and 'how long,' are finally answered, and the one who inclined His ear to the humble will dwell among them, Revelation 21:3. What Psalm 10 could only ask is then simply the case: no man of the earth will ever strike terror again.

quiz.q: What is David's opening complaint in Psalm 10:1?

options.text: That God seems to stand far off and hide Himself in times of trouble.
options.note: This is the psalm's direct opening question and complaint.

options.text: That his enemies have already been defeated.
options.note: The complaint is the opposite; the wicked are actively prospering while God seems absent.

options.text: That he has lost his kingdom.
options.note: The complaint concerns God's felt distance, not a specific loss of political power.

options.text: Nothing; the psalm opens in confident praise.
options.note: Verse 1 is an anguished question, not confident praise; that shift happens later in the psalm.

quiz.q: What does the wicked man say to himself, according to verses 6 and 11?

options.text: That he will never be moved and that God has forgotten and does not see.
options.note: This double quotation exposes the wicked man's arrogant, practical denial of God's justice and attention.

options.text: That he fears God's coming judgment.
options.note: The wicked man's inner speech expresses the opposite, confident denial that judgment will ever come.

options.text: That he plans to repent soon.
options.note: No such intention is described; his inner speech is arrogant self-assurance, not repentance.

options.text: Nothing is quoted from the wicked man's thoughts.
options.note: Verses 6 and 11 both directly quote the wicked man's inner thoughts.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe the wicked man's treatment of the helpless in verses 8-10?

options.text: He lies in wait like a lion, ambushing and preying on the innocent, oppressed, and lowly.
options.note: This vivid predatory imagery describes the wicked man's violence against the vulnerable.

options.text: He generously provides for the poor.
options.note: This is the opposite of the psalm's description, which portrays predatory violence against the helpless.

options.text: He ignores the poor entirely, neither helping nor harming them.
options.note: The passage describes active predation and ambush, not mere indifference.

options.text: The psalm gives no description of his actions.
options.note: Verses 8-10 give a detailed, vivid description of his predatory behavior.

quiz.q: What does David affirm about God in verse 14, despite the earlier complaint?

options.text: That God has in fact regarded trouble and grief and will repay it by His hand; He is the helper of the fatherless.
options.note: This is the psalm's turning point, affirming God's actual attentiveness despite how distant He may feel.

options.text: That God truly has forgotten the oppressed forever.
options.note: This is precisely what the psalm rejects; verse 14 affirms God has in fact regarded trouble and grief.

options.text: That justice will only come in the afterlife, never in history.
options.note: The psalm does not specify only an afterlife resolution; it affirms God's active attentiveness and coming action generally.

options.text: Nothing about God's attentiveness is affirmed here.
options.note: Verse 14 makes a direct, positive affirmation about God regarding trouble and grief.

quiz.q: How does the psalm close in verses 16-18?

options.text: With confidence that the LORD is King forever, who hears the humble and vindicates the fatherless and oppressed.
options.note: This is the psalm's confident resolution after the earlier lament.

options.text: In continued despair with no resolution.
options.note: The psalm moves to confident affirmation of God's kingship and justice by its close, not unresolved despair.

options.text: With a call for Israel to take up arms against the nations.
options.note: The closing confession is about God's eternal kingship and care for the oppressed, not a military call to arms.

options.text: The psalm has no closing section.
options.note: Verses 16-18 form a clear, deliberate closing confession of trust.

questions: David honestly asks God why He seems far off while evil prospers. Is there a situation in your life right now where you feel God is distant, and what would it look like to bring that question honestly to Him rather than suppress it?

The wicked man in this psalm convinces himself that God does not see and will never call him to account. Where might you be tempted to act as though God is not watching, even while maintaining outward religious appearances?
The psalm describes real predatory harm done to the helpless and vulnerable. Who around you is currently vulnerable or being taken advantage of, and how might God be calling you to stand with them?
Despite the earlier complaint, David affirms that God has in fact regarded trouble and grief. What past evidence of God's attentiveness can you hold onto when He currently feels distant?

The psalm ends with confidence in God's eternal kingship rather than an explanation of why evil was allowed to continue. How does trusting God's ultimate reign, rather than needing every question answered now, change the way you wait through unresolved injustice?

translationNotes.note: This psalm carries no title of its own, likely because it originally formed one composition with Psalm 9 as part of a continuous alphabetic acrostic, a unity the Greek Septuagint preserves by numbering the two together as a single psalm.
He hides His face and never sees quotes the wicked man's own cynical reasoning, not a statement of fact; the psalm's later verses directly refute this claim about God.
The humble renders anavim, a term for those bent low by affliction or oppression who depend wholly on God, a recurring category of person across the Psalms whom God specifically favors and hears.
